Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile clinically with the indexed trauma and the rest of the profile. It implies danger from interpersonal or environmental attack rather than illness-related threat, with no supporting triggers, memory, or appraisal content indicating assault-related fear.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: Scanning for exits and being unable to believe reassurance about safety can occur in severe PTSD, but together they suggest a persistent external attack/escape-based threat style that fits poorly with a life-threatening illness trauma unless there is clear accompanying illness-specific danger content. No such illness-linked threat items are present.

issues.item: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because it omits Triggers and Memory entirely despite an extreme PTSD severity (PCL-5=73) and instead concentrates on severe Threat, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies without any plausible illness-linked intrusion or cue structure.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is poorly matched to a life-threatening illness trauma and points toward an assault/accident-type fear context rather than medical trauma; this clashes with 'Avoid Medical Cues' which is the trauma-congruent avoidance item.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: 'Dissociate Deliberately' is possible in PTSD, but paired here with strongly illness-specific avoidance and no memory/trigger content, it suggests a different symptom profile and lacks support from the stated formulation, which centers Threat–Appraisal–Strategy cycling rather than dissociative disengagement.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is not well aligned with the trauma type of life-threatening illness. The example implies a threat context more typical of assault/accident trauma, while the rest of the profile centers on medical cues.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Medical Cues' and 'Avoid Thinking' fit illness trauma, but 'Avoid Circumstances ... being in the dark' pulls toward a different trauma context, reducing within-node coherence.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: Cross-node coherence is weakened because the threat items emphasize generalized danger and delays, while the negative appraisals are purely global self-defectiveness/weakness with no illness-related or health-related meaning. For life-threatening illness, some link is expected between medical threat and appraisals; these items instead suggest a different or more diffuse formulation.

vignette:
Kai, a 35-year-old UX designer, found his world irrevocably altered two years ago when a sudden, aggressive autoimmune flare-up landed him in the ICU. He remembered the rapid onset of symptoms – a crushing fatigue, then searing pain, followed by a terrifying inability to breathe properly. The days blurred into a haze of beeping machines, urgent voices, and the constant, chilling awareness that his body was failing him. There were moments when he truly believed he wouldn't make it, the fragility of his existence laid bare. He endured weeks of uncertainty, a period during which his wife was told to prepare for the worst, before a slow, arduous recovery began.

Even after his discharge and the doctors’ assurances of his physical recovery, Kai’s body retained a profound memory of the ordeal. He now felt a constant tension, a persistent thrum of readiness, as if his system was perpetually on high alert, poised to react to an invisible danger. This pervasive sense of his body feeling constantly tense and ready to react to danger made it difficult to relax, even at home with his wife. The experience had also left him with a deep-seated conviction that there was something inherently wrong with him as a person. His own body, once reliable, had betrayed him so profoundly that he had come to believe he was fundamentally defective, seeing himself as a weak person unable to withstand the hidden threats of life. To cope with the overwhelming fear and the crushing weight of this self-perception, Kai found himself retreating into a profound emotional numbness, a feeling of being dead inside, disconnected from the vibrant person he once was.

This internal landscape began to dictate his external life. He started to actively avoid anything that reminded him of his time in the hospital. Driving past the medical center where he received treatment became an unbearable ordeal, prompting him to take lengthy detours on his commute to his design studio. The distant wail of an ambulance siren would send a jolt of panic through him, making his heart race and his hands clammy. He meticulously avoided physical examinations, postponing check-ups and finding excuses not to see his general practitioner, terrified of triggering memories or discovering a new vulnerability. He also developed an intense aversion to any situation that put his body under stress. His previously active lifestyle, which included regular cycling and gym visits, dwindled. Even a brisk walk could make him anxious, the feeling of his heart rate increasing or his breath quickening triggering a primal fear that his body was once again on the brink of collapse.

At work, Kai’s role as a UX designer often involved collaborative projects with tight deadlines. If a client or a team member’s response took longer than expected, his mind would immediately catastrophize, convinced something bad was happening, a critical error, a project failure, or worse, a personal attack. This constant internal alarm made him irritable and less effective. Despite repeated reassurances from his wife, his doctors, and even his therapist that he was now safe and healthy, he found it impossible to genuinely believe it. The memory of his vulnerability was too vivid, too real. He actively avoided thinking about the event, pushing away any intrusive images of the ICU, the sterile smells, the fear in his wife's eyes. He hoped that if he ignored it long enough, it would simply fade away.

Over the past months, these avoidance patterns had solidified into routines, slowly constricting his life. His emotional numbness had created a chasm between him and his wife, who struggled to understand his increasing withdrawal. His work performance, once meticulous and creative, now suffered under the weight of his constant vigilance and the exhausting effort of avoiding triggers. The cumulative strain of living in a state of perpetual alert, coupled with the belief in his own inherent weakness and defectiveness, eventually brought Kai to seek help. He was tired of feeling dead inside, tired of the constant fear, and desperately hoped to find a way back to the person he used to be, before his body betrayed him.
